title: The Buddha's Last Days
bigQuestion: What does the account of the Buddha's death teach its readers about how a community goes on without its teacher?

story.title: Three Times He Asked
story.kicker: An old teacher lies between two trees and gives his students one more chance to ask.
paragraphs: The sutta sets the scene in a grove of sal trees near Kusinara, a small town in northern India. The Buddha, now about eighty years old in the tradition's telling, is lying on his right side between two trees. The text says the trees burst into bloom out of season, and flowers fell on his body.

Monks have gathered. Ananda, his cousin and attendant for many years, has already gone off to weep. He leaned on a door frame, the text says, and cried that his teacher was passing away before his own training was complete. The Buddha sent for him and praised his years of kindness.

Now the Buddha turns to all the monks. It may be, he says, that one of you has a doubt about the Buddha, the teaching or the community. Ask now, so you will not regret later that you had the chance and missed it. No one speaks. He asks a second time. Silence. He asks a third time. Still no one speaks.

Then, the sutta says, he gives his final words. This chapter reads the Book of the Great Decease, Digha Nikaya 16, in T.W. Rhys Davids' 1881 translation. It is the longest sutta in the Pali Canon, and one of the most loved.
story.think: Why might a teacher ask three times for questions, and what does the silence suggest?

sections.title: The Book of the Great Decease

lessons.title: The Longest Sutta
lessons.mainIdea: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 16, tells the Buddha's final journey and death as the tradition remembers it.
reading: The *Mahaparinibbana Sutta* is the sixteenth discourse in the Digha Nikaya, the Long Discourses. Its name means the great discourse on the final nibbana. Rhys Davids called it the Book of the Great Decease in Sacred Books of the East 11 (1881), and divided it into six chapters with numbered verses.

The sutta follows the Buddha's last months. He travels from Rajagaha north toward Kusinara, stopping in towns and teaching along the way. He falls ill, recovers, eats a final meal, and dies. Then the text describes the funeral and how the relics were shared. Few suttas follow a story over so many places and weeks.

Scholars think the sutta grew over time. Parts may be very early, and others were likely added as the community developed. Versions survive in Chinese and Sanskrit too, which lets scholars compare. For Buddhists, it is the account of the *parinibbana*, the final passing of one who has already reached nibbana.

words.d: Digha Nikaya 16, the long account of the Buddha's last journey and death
final nibbana; the death of an awakened person, as Buddhists describe it
the Long Discourses, a collection of 34 long suttas in the Pali Canon

look.title: The Book in Rhys Davids' Chapters
rows: Chapter 2: illness at Beluva, 'be ye lamps'
Chapter 3: giving up the will to live
look.cite: Book of the Great Decease, tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, SBE 11 (1881)
look.prompt: In which chapter would you look for the Buddha's final words?

check.q: What does parinibbana mean?
choices: The final passing of an awakened person
check.why: Parinibbana is final nibbana, the death of one who has already awakened, as Buddhists describe it.

check.q: Where in the Pali Canon is this sutta?
check.why: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta is Digha Nikaya 16.

check.q: Why do scholars think the sutta grew over time?
choices: It has layers and parallel versions that differ
It was written in English first
check.why: Comparison of Pali, Chinese and Sanskrit versions suggests layers added over time.

lessons.title: Seven Conditions of Welfare
lessons.mainIdea: Early in the sutta, the Buddha lists conditions that keep a community strong, first for a people and then for monks.
reading: The sutta opens with politics. King Ajatasattu of Magadha plans to attack the Vajjians, a people governed by assemblies. He sends a minister to ask the Buddha's view. The Buddha, as the text presents him, does not answer directly. He asks Ananda questions about the Vajjians instead.

Do they meet often and in full numbers? Do they meet in harmony and act in harmony? Do they respect their elders and their customs? Do they honor their shrines and protect holy people? As long as they do, the Buddha says, they may be expected to prosper. These are the seven *conditions of welfare*.

Then he gathers the monks and gives them a parallel list for the *sangha*. Meet often. Meet and act in harmony. Keep the rules. Respect elders. Readers often note the link: the sutta that ends with the teacher's death opens with how a group stays whole. The Vinaya-minded tradition read this as guidance for the order after him.

words.d: the seven habits the sutta says keep a people or a monastic community strong
the community of Buddhist monks and nuns
a people of ancient northern India who governed by assemblies

look.title: A Community Checklist
look.text: Meet often and in full numbers. Meet in harmony, act in harmony, and part in harmony. Keep what has been agreed. Honor elders. The sutta gives these to the Vajjians and then, in parallel form, to the monks.
look.prompt: Why might a text about a teacher's death begin with advice on how a group holds together?

check.q: Who plans to attack the Vajjians at the start of the sutta?
check.why: Ajatasattu of Magadha sends a minister to ask about his planned attack.

check.q: What is one condition of welfare the sutta names?
check.why: The conditions include meeting often and acting in harmony.

check.q: What does the Buddha do after answering about the Vajjians?
choices: Gives a parallel list for the monks
Writes a letter to the king
check.why: He gathers the monks and gives conditions of welfare for the sangha.

lessons.title: No Closed Fist
lessons.mainIdea: In the sutta, the Buddha says he has held nothing back and does not see himself as the one who leads the order.
reading: At Beluva the Buddha falls seriously ill. When he recovers, Ananda says he was comforted by the thought that the Buddha would not pass away without leaving instructions for the order. The Buddha's reply, as the text gives it, is one of the most quoted passages in the sutta.

He says he has taught without any difference between inner and outer teachings. The teacher, he says, has no closed fist that keeps some things back. He adds that he does not think of himself as the one who leads the order or that the order depends on him. So why would he leave special instructions?

Readers have taken this in several ways. Theravada teachers see it as a sign that the Pali teachings are complete and open. Some Mahayana and Vajrayana traditions, which value later or esoteric teachings, read the passage in its context: the Buddha held back nothing his listeners needed. Scholars note it as a clue to early debates over authority.

words.d: the sutta's image for a teacher who keeps some teachings secret
meant for a small group of trained students rather than everyone
the right to decide what counts as true teaching or proper practice

look.title: The Teacher's Open Hand
look.text: The Buddha tells Ananda that he has taught the truth without separating inner from outer doctrine, and that the Tathagata has nothing like the closed fist of a teacher who keeps some things back.
look.cite: Book of the Great Decease 2.32, Digha Nikaya 16; paraphrased from tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, SBE 11 (1881)
look.prompt: What is the closed fist, and why would the Buddha, as the text presents him, deny having one?

check.q: What does the 'closed fist' stand for in the sutta?
choices: A way of begging for food
A teacher who keeps some teachings back
check.why: The Buddha says he has no closed fist of a teacher who keeps some things back.

check.q: Where does the Buddha fall ill in chapter 2?
check.why: Rhys Davids' chapter 2 places the illness at the village of Beluva.

check.q: How do some Mahayana readers handle this passage?
choices: They read it in context: nothing his listeners needed was held back
They say the sutta is not Buddhist
check.why: Traditions that value later teachings read the line as about what those listeners needed.

lessons.title: Be Ye Lamps
lessons.mainIdea: The Buddha tells Ananda to be a lamp and a refuge to himself, with the Dhamma as lamp and refuge.
reading: The passage right after the closed fist gives the sutta's best-known line. The Buddha, as the text presents him, says he is old and his body is worn like a cart held together with straps. Therefore, he tells Ananda, be lamps unto yourselves. Be a refuge to yourselves. Hold fast to the truth as a lamp and as a refuge.

The Pali word dipa can mean lamp or island. Rhys Davids chose lamp. Many modern translators, such as Maurice Walshe (1987), choose island: be an island to yourselves, a safe place in a flood. Both readings make sense. A lamp gives light to see by. An island gives safe ground. The translator's choice colors the verse.

The line does not tell Ananda to rely on himself instead of the teaching. It pairs self and *Dhamma*: take the self as refuge, and the Dhamma as refuge, nothing else. The sutta then explains how: through mindfulness of body, feelings, mind and mental objects. Teachers across schools quote this passage when students fear losing a teacher.

words.d: a Pali word that can mean lamp or island; translators differ
a place of safety or support; Buddhists speak of taking refuge in the Three Jewels
sati: steady awareness of body, feelings, mind and mental objects, as the suttas describe it

look.title: Lamps unto Yourselves
look.text: Therefore, O Ananda, be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves. Betake yourselves to no external refuge. Hold fast to the truth as a lamp. Hold fast as a refuge to the truth.
look.cite: Book of the Great Decease 2.33, Digha Nikaya 16, tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist Suttas, SBE 11 (1881)
look.prompt: The passage names two refuges. What are they, and why might the sutta name both?

check.q: What two meanings can the Pali word dipa have?
check.why: Dipa can be lamp (Rhys Davids) or island (many modern translators).

check.q: Which two refuges does the passage name?
check.why: The Buddha says to take oneself as refuge and the truth, the Dhamma, as refuge.

check.q: What image does the Buddha use for his aging body in this passage?
choices: A worn cart held together with straps
check.why: The sutta compares his body to an old cart kept going with straps.

lessons.title: Ananda's Grief
lessons.mainIdea: The sutta shows Ananda weeping and the Buddha comforting him, a scene readers value for its honesty.
reading: Ananda is the most human figure in the sutta. He was the Buddha's cousin and his attendant for about twenty-five years, tradition says. At Kusinara, the text says, he went into a building, leaned against the door frame and wept. He had not yet reached awakening, and his teacher was leaving.

The Buddha sends for him. As the text gives it, he tells Ananda not to weep. Has he not taught that we must part from all that is dear? Whatever is born must end. Then he praises Ananda to the monks. For years, he says, Ananda served him with kind acts, kind words and kind thoughts. He tells Ananda to keep striving, and he will soon be free.

Buddhist readers draw two lessons. The teaching on impermanence holds even for the Buddha. And grief is met with kindness, not scolding. Tradition adds that Ananda reached awakening on the night before the *First Council*, where he recited the suttas from memory. So the one who wept becomes the one who keeps the teaching.

words.d: the Buddha's cousin and attendant; tradition says he recited the suttas at the First Council
anicca: the teaching that everything that begins also changes and ends
the gathering tradition places soon after the Buddha's death, where monks recited the teachings

look.title: Grief and Comfort
look.text: Ananda weeps against a door frame. The Buddha sends for him, reminds him that all that is dear must part, and then praises his years of kindness in front of the other monks.
look.prompt: Why might the sutta pair a hard teaching with public praise? What does that show about the teacher as the text presents him?

check.q: Why, according to the sutta, does Ananda weep?
choices: His teacher is dying and his own training is not complete
check.why: Ananda grieves that his teacher is passing while he is still a learner.

check.q: What does the Buddha praise in Ananda?
choices: Years of kind acts, words and thoughts
check.why: The Buddha praises Ananda's long service in body, speech and mind.

check.q: What role does tradition give Ananda after the Buddha's death?
choices: He recites the suttas at the First Council
check.why: Tradition says Ananda recited the discourses at the First Council.

lessons.title: The Dhamma as Teacher
lessons.mainIdea: Before he dies, the Buddha says his teaching and discipline will be the monks' teacher after him.
reading: Near the end, the Buddha anticipates a worry. Some may think, he says, that the word of the Teacher is ended and they have no teacher. They should not think so. The truths and the rules he has taught, the *Dhamma* and the *Vinaya*, will be their teacher after he is gone.

This answers the question the sutta has asked from its start: who leads when the leader is gone? The answer is not a successor. It is a body of teaching and a code of discipline. Buddhist communities read this as the reason the texts matter so much. The recited words take the place of the living teacher.

Different traditions built on this in different ways. Theravada monasteries center the Vinaya and the suttas. Many Mahayana and Vajrayana communities also stress living teachers and lineages, while honoring the texts. Zen speaks of transmission from teacher to student. Each claims continuity with the Buddha, but they locate it in different places.

words.d: the Buddhist code of discipline for monks and nuns, one of the Three Baskets
the Buddha's teaching; dharma in Sanskrit
a chain of teachers and students that a tradition traces back over time

look.title: Your Teacher After Me
look.text: The Buddha tells Ananda that the truths and the rules of the order which he has taught and laid down will be their Teacher after he is gone.
look.cite: Book of the Great Decease 6.1, Digha Nikaya 16; paraphrased from tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, SBE 11 (1881)
look.prompt: How does this answer the question of who leads the community after the Buddha?

check.q: What does the Buddha say will be the monks' teacher after him?
check.why: The sutta says the teaching and the discipline will be the teacher.

check.q: What is the Vinaya?
choices: The code of discipline for monks and nuns
check.why: The Vinaya is the monastic discipline, one of the Three Baskets.

check.q: How do many Mahayana and Vajrayana communities add to this idea?
choices: They also stress living teachers and lineages
check.why: They honor texts while also stressing living teachers and lineages of transmission.

sections.title: The Last Meal and Last Words

lessons.title: Cunda's Meal
lessons.mainIdea: The Buddha eats a final meal from Cunda the smith, falls ill, and then makes sure Cunda is not blamed.
reading: At Pava, a smith named Cunda invites the Buddha and the monks for a meal. The text says Cunda served a dish called sukara-maddava. The Buddha asks that it be served only to him and that the rest be buried. After eating, he falls ill with severe pain, but he continues on toward Kusinara.

The dish's name is uncertain. It may mean something like pig's delight. Rhys Davids translated it as dried boar's flesh, a common reading. Other readers, ancient and modern, think it was a kind of mushroom or a food that pigs like. The Pali commentaries already record different views. Scholars today still do not agree.

What the sutta stresses is Cunda. The Buddha tells Ananda that some may blame Cunda. He should be told instead that his gift carries great merit. Two meals, the text says, are equal in fruit: the one before the Buddha's awakening and the one before his final passing. Readers see this as care for a layperson's feelings, even at the end.

words.d: the smith at Pava who, the sutta says, served the Buddha his last meal
good karma that Buddhists believe comes from generous and kind actions
a Buddhist who is not a monk or nun

look.title: An Uncertain Dish
look.text: The Pali name is sukara-maddava. Rhys Davids (1881): dried boar's flesh. Other readers: a mushroom, or a soft food pigs enjoy. The commentaries list more than one view. The text itself does not say.
look.prompt: Why is it better to report the range of readings than to pick one here?

check.q: Who served the Buddha his last meal, according to the sutta?
check.why: Cunda the smith at Pava served the final meal.

check.q: Why is the name of the dish uncertain?
choices: The Buddha refused to name it
It is written in Chinese only
The Pali word can be read in more than one way
check.why: Sukara-maddava has been read as pork, mushroom or other foods since the commentaries.

check.q: What does the Buddha ask Ananda to tell Cunda?
choices: That his gift carries great merit
That he should leave the village
That he caused harm on purpose
That he must become a monk
check.why: The Buddha says Cunda's gift equals in merit the meal before his awakening.

lessons.title: Compounded Things Decay
lessons.mainIdea: The Buddha's last words, as the sutta records them, are that all compounded things decay and his followers should strive with diligence.
reading: After asking three times for questions and hearing none, the Buddha speaks his last words. Rhys Davids renders them: decay is inherent in all component things; work out your salvation with diligence. In Pali, the words are short: vayadhamma sankhara, appamadena sampadetha.

*Sankhara* means things that are put together, formed or conditioned. Rhys Davids calls them component things. The claim is that anything made of parts will come apart. *Appamada* means heedfulness or diligence, not being careless. The Dhammapada's second chapter praises the same quality. Salvation is Rhys Davids' word; many modern translators prefer strive or bring about the goal.

Readers note how the last words gather the sutta's themes. The body is like the worn cart. The dear must part. Even the Buddha's life is conditioned and ends. Yet the response is not despair. It is effort. The sutta then describes him entering deep meditative states and passing away, as its tellers remember.

words.d: formed or conditioned things; anything made of parts
heedfulness or diligence; not being careless
depending on causes and parts, and so bound to change

look.title: The Last Words
look.text: Behold now, brethren, I exhort you, saying, 'Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!'
look.cite: Book of the Great Decease 6.10, Digha Nikaya 16, tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist Suttas, SBE 11 (1881)
look.prompt: The first half states a fact; the second gives an instruction. How does the first lead to the second?

check.q: What does sankhara mean in the last words?
choices: Things that are put together or conditioned
check.why: Sankhara are formed or conditioned things; Rhys Davids calls them component things.

check.q: What quality do the last words ask for?
check.why: Appamada means heedfulness or diligence.

check.q: What happens just before the last words?
choices: The Buddha asks three times for questions and no one speaks
check.why: He invites questions three times, hears none, then speaks.

lessons.title: Dividing the Relics
lessons.mainIdea: The sutta ends with the cremation and the sharing of relics among eight groups who build stupas.
reading: The last chapter describes the funeral. The Mallas of Kusinara honor the body for six days with music, garlands and perfume, the text says. The body is cremated. Then kings and clans from other regions send messengers. Each claims a share of the remains, and a dispute threatens.

A brahmin named Dona calms them. The Buddha taught patience, he reminds them. It would not be right to fight over his remains. He divides the relics into eight equal portions. Each group takes one home and builds a *stupa*, a mound for relics. Dona keeps the vessel, and a late arrival takes the ashes of the fire.

The sutta says the Buddha had earlier told Ananda that his remains should be treated like those of a universal king, with a stupa at a crossroads. Buddhists across Asia have built stupas ever since. Archaeologists at Piprahwa, in India, found a relic vessel in 1898 with an inscription that many scholars read as naming the Buddha's relics.

words.d: remains of a holy person, such as bones or ashes, kept and honored
a dome-shaped monument that holds relics; Buddhists honor it by walking around it
burning a body as part of a funeral

look.title: How the Remains Were Shared
look.cite: Book of the Great Decease 6.58-6.62, Digha Nikaya 16, tr. Rhys Davids, SBE 11 (1881)
look.prompt: Why might the sutta record these counts so carefully?

check.q: Who divides the relics, according to the sutta?
check.why: Dona reminds the claimants of the Buddha's patience and divides the relics into eight.

check.q: What is a stupa?
check.why: A stupa is a mound or dome built over relics.

check.q: How many equal portions of relics does the sutta describe?
check.why: Dona makes eight equal portions.

lessons.title: Four Places to Visit
lessons.mainIdea: The sutta names four places a devoted person may visit: where the Buddha was born, awakened, first taught and passed away.
reading: In chapter 5, Ananda worries that after the Buddha's death the monks will no longer see him. The Buddha, as the text presents him, names four places worth visiting with reverence. Where the Buddha was born. Where he awakened. Where he set the wheel of the Dhamma in motion. Where he passed away.

Buddhists identify these as Lumbini, in today's Nepal; Bodh Gaya; Sarnath; and Kusinara, today Kushinagar. All four are still *pilgrimage* sites. Pilgrims from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Japan, Tibet and the United States visit them. The emperor Ashoka marked Lumbini with a pillar in the third century BCE, and its inscription names the place as the Buddha's birthplace.

The passage shows the sutta thinking ahead. The teacher will be gone, but places can hold his memory. The text says those who die while on such a journey with a devoted heart will be reborn in a heavenly world. Buddhists read the four places as reminders; the practices at them are described in guides to Buddhist pilgrimage.

words.d: a journey to a holy place for religious reasons
the place in today's Nepal where Buddhists say the Buddha was born
the modern name of Kusinara, where the sutta says the Buddha passed away

look.title: Four Places, Four Events
look.text: Lumbini: birth. Bodh Gaya: awakening. Sarnath: first sermon. Kushinagar: final passing. The sutta itself does not name the towns in this passage; it names the events, and Buddhists match them to places.
look.prompt: Why might a text name events rather than towns? What does that allow later readers to do?

check.q: Which event does the sutta connect with the third place?
choices: Setting the wheel of the Dhamma in motion
check.why: The third place is where the Buddha first taught, Sarnath.

check.q: Where is Lumbini today?
check.why: Lumbini is in southern Nepal; Ashoka's pillar there names it the birthplace.

check.q: Why does Ananda raise the question of places?
choices: He wants to build a palace
He worries the monks will no longer see the Buddha
He wants to leave the order
check.why: Ananda asks what monks will do once they can no longer see the Buddha.

review.q: What does the Mahaparinibbana Sutta describe?
choices: The Buddha's last journey and death
review.why: Digha Nikaya 16 tells of the final journey, death and funeral.

review.q: In Rhys Davids' translation, what does the Buddha tell Ananda to be?
review.why: Book of the Great Decease 2.33: 'be ye lamps unto yourselves.'

review.q: Why do some modern translations say 'island' instead of 'lamp'?
choices: The Pali word dipa can mean either
The sutta names a real island
review.why: Dipa can mean lamp or island.

review.q: What do the last words say about compounded things?
review.why: 6.10: decay is inherent in all component things.

review.q: What does the Buddha say will teach the monks after him?
review.why: 6.1: the truths and rules he taught will be their teacher.

review.q: How does the Buddha treat Cunda after the meal?
choices: He says Cunda's gift brings great merit
review.why: He tells Ananda to assure Cunda his gift was of great merit.

review.q: How many times does the Buddha ask for questions before his last words?
review.why: He asks three times, and the monks stay silent.

review.q: What do the eight groups build for their share of relics?
review.why: Each group builds a stupa over its portion.
